summary: Give the MELD calculator the bilirubin, the creatinine, the INR and the sodium and it returns MELD score (Using the original formula). It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the MELD calculator work?
sections.html:
The MELD calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports MELD score (Using the original formula) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the bilirubin, the creatinine, the INR and the sodium.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the MELD calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

MELD score=the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (189 ÷ 50) × the natural log of (bilirubin) + (957 ÷ 100) × the natural log of (creatinine) + (56 ÷ 5) × the natural log of (INR) + 643 ÷ 100))
MELD score=the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (33 ÷ 1000) × the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (189 ÷ 50) × the natural log of (bilirubin) + (957 ÷ 100) × the natural log of (creatinine) + (56 ÷ 5) × the natural log of (INR) + 643 ÷ 100)) × the smaller of (137, the larger of (125, sodium)) − 3521 ÷ 1000 × the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (189 ÷ 50) × the natural log of (bilirubin) + (957 ÷ 100) × the natural log of (creatinine) + (56 ÷ 5) × the natural log of (INR) + 643 ÷ 100)) − 33 ÷ 25 × the smaller of (137, the larger of (125, sodium)) + 4521 ÷ 25))
Mortality=(the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (189 ÷ 50) × the natural log of (bilirubin) + (957 ÷ 100) × the natural log of (creatinine) + (56 ÷ 5) × the natural log of (INR) + 643 ÷ 100)))
Mortality=(the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (33 ÷ 1000) × the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (189 ÷ 50) × the natural log of (bilirubin) + (957 ÷ 100) × the natural log of (creatinine) + (56 ÷ 5) × the natural log of (INR) + 643 ÷ 100)) × the smaller of (137, the larger of (125, sodium)) − 3521 ÷ 1000 × the larger of (1, the smaller of (40, (189 ÷ 50) × the natural log of (bilirubin) + (957 ÷ 100) × the natural log of (creatinine) + (56 ÷ 5) × the natural log of (INR) + 643 ÷ 100)) − 33 ÷ 25 × the smaller of (137, the larger of (125, sodium)) + 4521 ÷ 25)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Bilirubin = 10, Creatinine = 10, INR = 10 and Sodium = 10. Working through the relationship above gives MELD score = 40.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: MELD score = 40 should be roughly the size you expected from Bilirubin = 10 and Creatinine = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The MELD calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the bilirubin, the creatinine and the INR — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the MELD calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns MELD score (Using the original formula), derived from the bilirubin, the creatinine and the INR. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the MELD calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the bilirubin, the creatinine, the INR and the sodium, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mortality (Using the original formula) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mortality (Using the original formula) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports MELD score = 40. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the MELD calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
